evidence.paraphrase: Father Brown insists the fatal blow was not a miracle but the result of a well-known natural law recognized by scientists.
evidence.quote: It is a matter of physical science. The blacksmith is mistaken, not perhaps in saying that the blow was divine, but certainly in saying that it came by a miracle. It was no miracle, doctor, except in so far as man is himself a miracle, with his strange and wicked and yet half-heroic heart. The force that smashed that skull was a force well known to scientists\u2014one of the most frequently debated of the laws of nature.

evidence.paraphrase: Father Brown explains that gravity accelerates a falling object so a small hammer dropped from the tower would strike with bullet-like force.
evidence.quote: he had in his hand one of the most awful engines of nature; I mean gravitation, that mad and quickening rush by which all earth\u2019s creatures fly back to her heart when released. See, the inspector is strutting just below us in the smithy. If I were to toss a pebble over this parapet it would be something like a bullet by the time it struck him. If I were to drop a hammer\u2014even a small hammer\u2014

evidence.paraphrase: The priest identifies an anomaly to investigate: why a small hammer was used to deliver such a powerful blow.
evidence.quote: There is at least the mystery of why so big a man should attempt so big a blow with so little a hammer.

evidence.paraphrase: The doctor reasons from physical lifting power to deduce which persons could have chosen and wielded the small hammer.
evidence.quote: It is not a question of force or courage between the sexes. It\u2019s a question of lifting power in the shoulders. A bold woman could commit ten murders with a light hammer and never turn a hair. She could not kill a beetle with a heavy one.

evidence.paraphrase: The doctor uses a distinctive anatomical detail to confirm the corpse's identity.
evidence.quote: I was the colonel\u2019s medical man, and I knew his body better than he did. He had very fine hands, but quite peculiar ones. The second and third fingers were the same length. Oh, that\u2019s the colonel right enough.

evidence.paraphrase: The doctor describes the extreme violence of the killing, with the skull shattered as if by a giant.
evidence.quote: It is inadequate to say that the skull was smashed to bits like an eggshell. Fragments of bone were driven into the body and the ground like bullets into a mud wall. It was the hand of a giant.

evidence.paraphrase: Wilfred reacts with superstitious dread and confusion to the nature of the death.
evidence.quote: A shudder of superstition went through the slight figure of the curate. \u201cI can hardly understand,\u201d he said.

evidence.paraphrase: Confronted with the truth, Wilfred attempts to throw himself from the tower and is caught.
evidence.quote: Wilfred Bohun threw one leg over the parapet, and Father Brown had him in a minute by the collar.

evidence.paraphrase: Father Brown contrasts the distorted perspective gained from height with that from the valley.
evidence.quote: One sees great things from the valley; only small things from the peak.

evidence.paraphrase: The narration emphasizes the disorienting reversal of scale seen from the church tower.
evidence.quote: the monstrous foreshortening and disproportion, the dizzy perspectives, the glimpses of great things small and small things great; a topsy-turvydom of stone in the mid-air.

evidence.paraphrase: Wilfred offers the theory that a madman in a fit could possess superhuman strength to explain the blow.
evidence.quote: have you never heard, doctor, that a maniac in his paroxysm may have the strength of ten men?

evidence.paraphrase: Wilfred reacts with terror to Father Brown's accurate reconstruction of the crime.
evidence.quote: \u201cHow do you know all this?\u201d he cried. \u201cAre you a devil?\u201d
